value_proposition_comparison.promise: [INFERENCE S2] "Run product development in one system, roadmap to release" — plan (projects, initiatives), build (issues, cycles) and release in one coherent product, with AI and analytics in the same workflow.
evidence: [FACT S2] Feature scope explicitly spans roadmap-to-release: projects and initiatives, issue tracking and cycles, mobile, AI workflows and agents, analytics.

[FACT S1] Published entitlements support the promise at Business: Triage Intelligence, Code Intelligence, Insights, Asks, Zendesk/Intercom, unlimited teams, private teams and guests at $16/user/mo billed yearly.
[FACT S1] Free tier (unlimited members, 2 teams, 250 issues) makes the promise testable at zero cost; paid entry at $10.
[FACT S3] Shipping evidence inside the window: 2026-10-22 changelog for Loops triggered by Slack and GitHub events, shareable templates, assignable reasoning levels.

[INFERENCE S3] Customer stories exist as a content category, but no named outcome metrics were captured, so the promise is evidenced by capability lists and shipping cadence rather than by quantified results.
value_proposition_comparison.mechanism: [INFERENCE S1, S2] Mechanism is consolidation on a shared data model: one object set (projects, initiatives, issues, cycles) means planning and execution are not synchronised between tools; intelligence features (Triage, Code, Insights) sit on that same data, and AI is invoked where work already happens — event triggers from Slack/GitHub, coding sessions inside the issue flow, credit-metered.
value_proposition_comparison.uniqueness: [INFERENCE S2, S3] Differentiated on development-native depth plus single-system scope. Not unique in offering AI (Asana ships AI too, S7) and not unique in intake breadth (Asana lists service/client management and forms, S4, S5); the claimed unique combination is engineering-grade build constructs plus code-level intelligence in one product. Uniqueness is asserted from vendor pages only — no independent verification [UNKNOWN].
value_proposition_comparison.weakest_link: [FACT S1] AI credit requirement for coding sessions and Loops with consumption pricing [UNKNOWN]; [INFERENCE] cross-functional launch artefacts (goals, resourcing, proofing) not evidenced in the sampled cards — adequacy [UNKNOWN], not proven absent.

value_proposition_comparison.promise: [INFERENCE S5, S7] "Coordinate the organisation's critical work in one governed system, with humans and AI agents working from shared plans, goals and context."
evidence: [FACT S4] Advanced publishes the constructs the promise relies on: portfolios, goals, portfolio resource management, approvals/proofing, time tracking, at $24.99/user/mo billed annually.
[FACT S5] Multiple product families are listed — agentic work management, service/client management, developer teams — which is what makes the breadth claim checkable rather than rhetorical.
[FACT S7] Q3 2026 release ships prebuilt AI Teammates, AI workflows across tools, shared context and governance, plus assignment automation and planning pages.

[FACT S4] AI allowances are published in units: five requests per user/month capped at 50 per account for AI Teammates and Dash; AI Studio 50K credits (Starter) / 75K (Advanced) per billing account/month.
[FACT S6, S7] Evaluation-grade proof formats exist: demo video, research report, calculator, templates, training, release kit and webinar. Outcome metrics and independent validation remain [UNKNOWN].
value_proposition_comparison.mechanism: [INFERENCE S4, S5, S7] Mechanism is alignment through shared context: goals and portfolios give a common hierarchy above projects, resource management and time tracking make capacity explicit, and AI agents are given the same plans and governance so cross-team work is coordinated rather than hand-translated. Governance is the control layer that makes org-wide agent use acceptable to risk-averse buyers.
value_proposition_comparison.uniqueness: [INFERENCE S5, S7] Differentiated on horizontal breadth plus an explicit governance narrative for AI at scale. Not unique in shipping AI features (Linear ships AI workflows, agents, Loops — S2, S3) and not unique in having intake (Linear Asks, Zendesk/Intercom — S1, S2). The claimed unique combination is function-agnostic scope with portfolio/goal constructs and governance in one platform. Vendor-asserted only [UNKNOWN].

narrative_analysis.villain: [INFERENCE S5, S7] Two villains: work sprawl across teams, functions and tools that leaves leaders without shared visibility, and ungoverned AI adoption that adds risk when agents act without shared context or controls.

positioning_axes.axis_x: Scope orientation: engineering build depth (left) ←→ cross-functional launch breadth (right)
positioning_axes.axis_y: Deployment weight: team-scale, self-serve simplicity (bottom) ←→ organisation-scale governance and administration (top)
positioning_axes.rationale: The buyer implied by request_brief is a PM coordinating product development and cross-functional launch planning for 20 people, with no company positioning supplied. Two questions actually decide that purchase and are the only ones the corpus differentiates cleanly: (1) does the product's centre of gravity sit in the build loop or in the cross-functional launch layer, and (2) does it assume team-scale self-serve adoption or organisation-scale rollout with governance and admin? Axis 1 is evidenced on both sides — Linear's scope is roadmap-to-release for software teams [S2], Asana's is cross-functional functions and leaders with a developer-team offering alongside [S5]. Axis 2 is also evidenced: Linear sells a per-team ladder with an unlimited-member free tier and enterprise controls behind custom pricing [S1], while Asana frames humans-and-agents coordination at organisational scale with governance as a release-level message [S5, S7]. Both axes are decision-relevant because entry-tier price is nearly level — $10 vs $10.99 per user/month, i.e. $2,400 vs $2,637.60 at 20 seats per year [S1, S4] — so scope and operating weight, not sticker price, are the tie-breakers. A third candidate axis, AI cost predictability, was rejected: credit consumption, overage and enterprise pricing are [UNKNOWN] for both vendors [S1, S4], so no honest placement is possible on it. Caveat: the axes are analyst-chosen, and the placements are inferences from vendor messaging, not from product testing.

placements.x_position: Left-of-centre: strongly engineering-build-oriented, with only partial cross-functional reach (Asks, customer requests, Zendesk/Intercom intake) [S1, S2]
placements.y_position: Low: team-scale and self-serve — free tier with unlimited members and 2 teams, per-team paid ladder, enterprise controls only at custom-priced Enterprise [S1]
placements.justification: [FACT S2] Scope is roadmap-to-release for software-building teams; [FACT S1] packaging is organised around teams, issues and per-user tiers with a self-serve free entry; [FACT S3] voice is changelog-led and practitioner-facing. Cross-functional launch constructs (goals, portfolios, resourcing, proofing) are not evidenced, so the placement stops short of the right-hand side [UNKNOWN].
placements.confidence: medium (inference from vendor pages; no product test)

placements.x_position: Right-of-centre: strongly cross-functional, spanning operations, marketing, IT and leaders across multiple product families [S5, S6]
placements.y_position: High: organisation-scale framing with goals, portfolios, resource management and AI governance as explicit messages [S4, S5, S7]
placements.justification: [FACT S5] Audience and product families are function-based and include leaders; [FACT S4] Advanced publishes portfolio, goal, resourcing, proofing and time-tracking constructs; [FACT S7] governance and shared context are release-level claims. Engineering-native depth is not evidenced even though a developer-team offering is listed [S5, UNKNOWN], so the placement stays right of the build axis rather than on it.
placements.confidence: medium (inference from vendor pages; org-scale framing is messaging, not measured implementation overhead)

positioning_axes.underserved_quadrant: Cross-functional launch breadth × team-scale simplicity — the lower-right quadrant: Asana-grade launch constructs (goals, portfolios, resourcing, approvals/proofing, time tracking) delivered without organisation-scale administration assumptions, at a 20-seat price and self-serve entry. Neither card set evidences a vendor centred there: Asana holds the breadth but frames it at organisational scale with governance [S5, S7] and gates goals/portfolios/resourcing to Advanced at $24.99 per user/month [S4]; Linear holds the team-scale, self-serve posture [S1] but its sampled scope is the engineering build loop [S2]. This is underserved in the corpus, not proven empty in the market — and with company_context null it cannot be claimed as 'our' quadrant. Mutual encroachment narrows the gap: Asana lists a developer-team offering [S5] and Linear sells cross-functional intake [S1, S2].
positioning_axes.caveat: Axes and placements are INFERENCE from seven paraphrased official pages dated 2026-10-27; no hands-on comparison, no win-loss or share data, so quadrant boundaries are indicative only.

quick_wins.action: Build the 20-seat comparison model with the unknowns left visible. Use the four published prices — Linear $10 and $16, Asana $10.99 and $24.99 per user/month billed annually [S1, S4] — compute 20 × 12, then add two blank lines for AI credit consumption and enterprise uplift so no unknown is silently set to zero.
quick_wins.why: The entry-tier gap is only $237.60 per year (about 9.9%) while the second tier gap is $2,157.60 (about 56.2%); a model makes the tier decision explicit rather than letting the seat price dominate.
quick_wins.success_measure: Every dollar in the model traces to S1 or S4, and every [UNKNOWN] is labelled

quick_wins.action: Write the team's real launch checklist before any demo, then mark each row as evidenced-in-corpus versus must-be-demonstrated: brief, dependencies, approvals/proofing, resourcing, time tracking, reporting, intake.
quick_wins.why: The corpus shows exactly where the two positions diverge: Linear evidences build constructs [S2] while Asana evidences goals, portfolios, resourcing, proofing and time tracking at Advanced [S4]; neither page can substitute for a workflow test.
quick_wins.success_measure: Checklist rows mapped to S1, S2 or S4, with an explicit 'not evidenced' bucket

quick_wins.action: Send both vendors one written question pack on the three unpriced variables: AI credit consumption and overage, enterprise banding, and SSO/SCIM timing — and require answers in writing before scoring.
quick_wins.why: Both vendors leave the same three numbers [UNKNOWN] (Linear credits and custom Enterprise [S1]; Asana request caps, credits and quote-only Enterprise [S4]), so written answers are the cheapest way to remove the largest source of budget error.
quick_wins.success_measure: Written responses on file for both vendors, or documented refusal

quick_wins.action: Split the 20 seats by need rather than by preference — build-loop seats (issues, cycles, triage, code intelligence) versus cross-functional seats (goals, portfolios, resourcing, proofing) — and map each subset to a published tier without assuming equivalence.
quick_wins.why: The plans are not feature-equivalent: Linear bundles intelligence at Business [S1] while Asana bundles planning and resourcing at Advanced [S4], so a uniform 20-seat purchase either overpays for build seats or under-covers launch seats.
quick_wins.success_measure: Each seat subset has a named tier or an explicit 'no evidenced home' flag

strategic_moves.action: Decide the structural question — one platform or two tools with the integration priced — and test the chosen posture on one real launch in a structured two-week pilot with exit criteria.
strategic_moves.why: The corpus supports two coherent but different bets: Linear as a single roadmap-to-release system for the build loop [S2, S3], or Asana as the cross-functional layer with goals, portfolios and resourcing [S4, S5] plus governance for agents [S7]. The handoff touchpoints that would carry a two-tool setup are nameable (Slack and GitHub triggers [S3]; cross-tool AI workflows [S7]) but their cost is [UNKNOWN], so the decision needs a test, not a page.
strategic_moves.success_measure: One launch completed with handoff count, approval cycle time and admin hours recorded for the chosen posture

strategic_moves.action: Set the AI governance and spend policy before choosing a tier, then check it against what each vendor actually publishes: Linear admin roles and enterprise controls [S1], Asana shared context and governance [S7].
strategic_moves.why: Asana is positioning governance as its differentiator for agent adoption [S7] while Linear ships agent controls and reasoning levels into the developer workflow [S3]; agreeing the team's own rules first prevents a governance narrative from deciding the purchase. Both vendors' credit economics stay [UNKNOWN] [S1, S4], so the policy must cap exposure rather than trust published allowances.
strategic_moves.success_measure: Written policy covering who may spend credits, which work agents may touch, and what control evidence is required — mapped to a published vendor entitlement, not a claim

confidence_flags.detail: Neither competitor's exact tagline is in the corpus; cards paraphrase. All tagline cells are labelled paraphrase and must not be quoted as vendor wording.

request_brief.company_context is null, so no 'Your Company' column exists and no baseline messaging, content estate or positioning was invented. Content-gap labels ('gap for us', 'opportunity for them', 'parity') therefore describe relative coverage between the two competitors and gaps in the sampled corpus; 'us' has no evidenced content estate to compare against.

Rows set 'parity' where both competitors evidence a topic or format, 'opportunity for them' where one competitor evidences it and the other's sampled cards are silent, and 'gap for us' where neither evidences it. Silence in a one-date index sample [S3, S6] is not proof of absence, and no frequency, traffic, ranking or engagement data was collected.

confidence_flags.item: Messaging scores (clarity, differentiation, proof, consistency, resonance)
confidence_flags.detail: All eight scores are labelled analyst opinion on a 1-5 scale derived from seven paraphrased pages. No third-party review, analyst report, win-loss or hands-on testing informed them; a different reviewer could score differently by a point or more.

The two axes were selected for decision relevance to a 20-person PM buyer, not derived statistically. Placements come from vendor messaging, not observed product behaviour; quadrant boundaries are indicative only. A rejected third axis (AI cost predictability) was excluded because both vendors leave credit and enterprise pricing [UNKNOWN].
confidence_flags.carried_from: Linear.sources [S1, S2, S3]; Asana.sources [S4, S5, S7]

confidence_flags.detail: Linear tone is inferred from a single index page [S3]; Asana tone from three pages [S5, S6, S7]. No ad copy testing, brand guidelines or audience research was available.

Both competitors' narratives are reconstructed from problem framing and themes in the cards; neither vendor publishes an explicit villain/hero story. Stakes are partly inferred from pricing mechanics (credits, tier gating) rather than from stated customer outcomes.

confidence_flags.item: AI credit consumption, overage and actual AI cost
confidence_flags.detail: Linear requires credits for coding sessions and Loops with consumption pricing unquantified [S1]; Asana publishes five requests per user/month capped at 50 per account plus 50K/75K AI Studio credits, with overage and add-ons unquantified [S4]. Do not treat published allowances as adequate at 20 seats.

Linear Enterprise is custom annual with SAML/SCIM and controls [S1]; Asana Enterprise requires a sales quote [S4]. Published tier comparisons stop applying if procurement or security review escalates the deal.

confidence_flags.item: Third-party reviews, complaint themes, analyst reports, win-loss, market share
confidence_flags.detail: No review sources are in the corpus and none were fetched by design; both competitors' recurring_complaint_themes_public_reviews are [UNKNOWN]. Any statement about customer sentiment, satisfaction or competitive win rates would be fabrication.

confidence_flags.item: SEO, traffic, social engagement, publishing cadence, company size and funding
confidence_flags.detail: No keyword, ranking, traffic, backlink, social or headcount/funding data exists in the corpus. Content observations are a one-date sample of index pages, so no claim is made about volume, frequency or performance.

Linear's cross-functional launch constructs and Asana's engineering-native depth are absent from the sampled cards, which is a corpus gap. Adequacy is [UNKNOWN] and must be demonstrated, not assumed absent.
